summary.text: Counting multiples of the order of \(2\bmod p\) among the product exponents and applying Legendre’s digit-sum formula gives the needed factorial divisibility, with a strict excess of \(p\)-adic valuation for every odd prime divisor of a composite \(n\); this forces that prime to divide both the quotient and a power of \(2\), while the remaining case \(n=2^j\) is ruled out by the exact computation \(v_2(a(2^j-1))=j-1\). Once \(n\) is prime, if the order of \(2\) were a proper divisor of \(n-1\), the corresponding factor \(2^d-1\) would make \(n\) divide the product numerator and hence the quotient, so the assumed congruence would force \(n\mid 2^{n-2}\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 P_m:=\prod_{1\le k<m}(2^k-1),\qquad N_m:=2^{m-1}P_m
\]
for every integer \(m\ge 1\). Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
 a(m)=\frac{N_m}{m!}=\frac{2^{m-1}}{m!}\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1).
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and establish the valuation estimates needed later.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). We use two standard facts.

First, if \(x=\sum_i e_i p^i\) is the base-\(p\) expansion of \(x\), and \(s_p(x)=\sum_i e_i\) is its base-\(p\) digit sum, then Legendre’s formula gives
\[
 v_p(x!)=\sum_{r\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{x}{p^r}\right\rfloor
       =\frac{x-s_p(x)}{p-1}.
\]
Indeed, summing the shifted base-\(p\) expansions of the floors \(\lfloor x/p^r\rfloor\) gives
\[
 (p-1)\sum_{r\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{x}{p^r}\right\rfloor=x-s_p(x).
\]
In particular, for \(x\ge1\), the digit sum is positive, so
\[
 (p-1)v_p(x!)<x. \tag{1}
\]

Second, for an odd prime \(p\), let
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]
be the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\). Since \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), \(d>0\), and Fermat’s theorem implies
\[
 d\mid p-1,
\]
so in particular \(d\le p-1\). Moreover,
\[
 d\mid k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2^k\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and hence \(p\mid 2^k-1\). Among the integers \(1,2,\ldots,m-1\), there are exactly \(\lfloor(m-1)/d\rfloor\) multiples of \(d\). Each corresponding factor in \(P_m\) contributes at least one factor of \(p\). Consequently
\[
 v_p(P_m)\ge \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{d}\right\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]

We now prove that \(a(m)\) is an integer. If \(p\) is an odd prime, (1) implies
\[
 v_p(m!)\le \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since \(d\le p-1\), division by \(d\) gives a quotient at least as large as division by \(p-1\). Therefore, by (2),
\[
 v_p(m!)
 \le \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 \le \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{d}\right\rfloor
 \le v_p(P_m)
 \le v_p(N_m). \tag{3}
\]
For \(p=2\), every factor \(2^k-1\) is odd, while (1) gives
\[
 v_2(m!)\le m-1=v_2(2^{m-1})=v_2(N_m). \tag{4}
\]
Thus, for every prime \(p\), the valuation of \(m!\) is at most that of \(N_m\). It follows that
\[
 m!\mid N_m.
\]
In particular, \(a(m)\) is a positive integer and satisfies the exact identity
\[
 N_m=a(m)m!. \tag{5}
\]

We next need a strict version of (3) in a special situation. Let \(p\ge3\) be prime, let \(b\ge2\), and put
\[
 m=pb-1.
\]
The least significant base-\(p\) digit of \(m\) is \(p-1\), because
\[
 pb-1=p(b-1)+(p-1).
\]
The remaining base-\(p\) digits are precisely the digits of \(b-1\). Since \(b-1>0\), their sum is at least \(1\). Hence
\[
 s_p(m)=(p-1)+s_p(b-1)\ge p. \tag{6}
\]
Legendre’s formula and (6) give
\[
 (p-1)v_p(m!)=m-s_p(m)\le m-p.
\]
It follows that
\[
 v_p(m!)\le \left\lfloor\frac{m-p}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
But
\[
 m-1=(m-p)+(p-1),
\]
so
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m-p}{p-1}\right\rfloor+1.
\]
Thus
\[
 v_p(m!)<\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
Combining this with \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\le p-1\) and (2), we obtain the strict inequality
\[
 v_p(m!)<v_p(P_m) \qquad(m=pb-1,\ b\ge2). \tag{7}
\]

Now suppose that \(n>2\) and
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{8}
\]
We first prove that \(n\) is prime. Assume, for contradiction, that \(n\) is composite.

There are two cases.

**Case 1: \(n\) has an odd prime divisor.**

Let \(q\ge3\) be a prime divisor of \(n\). Since \(n\) is composite, \(q<n\): if \(q=n\), then \(n\) itself would be prime. Write
\[
 n=qb.
\]
Because \(q<n\), we have \(b\ge2\). Put \(m=n-1=qb-1\). By (7),
\[
 v_q(m!)<v_q(P_m). \tag{9}
\]
Since \(q\) is odd, \(q\nmid2\), and therefore
\[
 v_q(N_m)=v_q(2^{m-1}P_m)=v_q(P_m).
\]
Using the exact identity (5), we also have
\[
 v_q(N_m)=v_q(a(m))+v_q(m!).
\]
Together with (9), this implies
\[
 v_q(a(m))>0,
\]
so
\[
 q\mid a(m)=a(n-1). \tag{10}
\]
On the other hand, \(q\mid n\), and (8) therefore gives
\[
 q\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Subtracting the divisibility (10), we conclude that
\[
 q\mid 2^{n-2}.
\]
Because \(q\) is prime, a prime dividing a power must divide its base; hence \(q\mid2\). This is impossible for \(q\ge3\).

**Case 2: \(n\) has no odd prime divisor.**

Then every prime divisor of \(n\) is \(2\). Therefore \(n\) is a power of \(2\):
\[
 n=2^j
\]
for some \(j\ge0\). One can see this directly by repeatedly dividing by a prime divisor: the only possible prime removed at each step is \(2\), and the process terminates at \(1\). Since \(n>2\), necessarily
\[
 j\ge2. \tag{11}
\]
Put
\[
 m=n-1=2^j-1.
\]
Every factor in \(P_m\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2(N_m)=v_2(2^{m-1}P_m)=m-1=2^j-2. \tag{12}
\]
The binary expansion of \(2^j-1\) consists of exactly \(j\) digits, all equal to \(1\). Thus
\[
 s_2(2^j-1)=j.
\]
Legendre’s formula yields
\[
 v_2(m!)=m-s_2(m)=2^j-1-j. \tag{13}
\]
From (5), (12), and (13),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_2(a(m))
 &=v_2(N_m)-v_2(m!)\\
 &=(2^j-2)-(2^j-1-j)\\
 &=j-1. \tag{14}
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(2^j\nmid a(m)\).

For \(j\ge2\), we also have
\[
 j\le2^j-2. \tag{15}
\]
This follows, for example, by induction: it is equality when \(j=2\), and if \(j\le2^j-2\), then
\[
 j+1\le 2^j-1\le2^{j+1}-2.
\]
By (15),
\[
 2^j\mid 2^{2^j-2}=2^{n-2}. \tag{16}
\]
But (8), together with (16), would then imply
\[
 2^j\mid a(n-1)=a(m),
\]
contradicting (14). This disposes of the second case.

Both possibilities for a composite \(n\) are impossible. Hence \(n\) is prime.

It remains to prove that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\). Since \(n>2\) is prime, \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(n\). Let
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2).
\]
The multiplicative group modulo \(n\) has order \(n-1\), so Lagrange’s theorem gives
\[
 d\mid n-1. \tag{17}
\]
We claim that \(d=n-1\). Suppose otherwise. Since \(d>0\), (17) makes \(d\) a proper positive divisor of \(n-1\), and therefore
\[
 1\le d<n-1. \tag{18}
\]
By the definition of multiplicative order,
\[
 2^d\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
 n\mid2^d-1. \tag{19}
\]
The inequality (18) shows that \(2^d-1\) occurs as one of the factors in
\[
 P_{n-1}=\prod_{1\le k<n-1}(2^k-1).
\]
Thus (19) implies
\[
 n\mid P_{n-1},
\]
and consequently
\[
 n\mid N_{n-1}=2^{n-2}P_{n-1}. \tag{20}
\]
By (5),
\[
 N_{n-1}=a(n-1)(n-1)!.
\]
Because \(n\) is prime, none of the factors \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\) is divisible by \(n\); hence
\[
 n\nmid(n-1)!.
\]
Euclid’s lemma applied to (20) therefore forces
\[
 n\mid a(n-1). \tag{21}
\]
Combining (21) with the original assumption (8) gives
\[
 n\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
Since \(n\) is prime, this implies \(n\mid2\), and hence \(n\le2\), contrary to \(n>2\). This contradiction proves
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_n(2)=n-1.
\]
Finally, for a prime \(n\), Euler’s totient is \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Therefore the order of \(2\) modulo \(n\) equals \(\varphi(n)\), which is exactly the assertion that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Thus every integer \(n>2\) satisfying
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
is prime, and \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).
